subsection: 5. Conflicts between economic interests and environmental interests

notes.h: Why conflicts arise
notes.b: Land, sea and resources can be used to make money or can be protected, and often they cannot do both at once. A conflict starts when people with economic interests and people with environmental interests want different things from the same place.
points: Economic interests are jobs, profit, energy supply, tax revenue, regional development (bringing investment to a poorer area) and infrastructure (roads, pipelines, power lines and similar). These are the reasons a project is proposed.
Environmental interests are habitats, landscape, heritage (historic and archaeological sites), water and air quality, health, safety and the climate. These are the reasons people object.
Interests conflict at local, national and global scales: a local community may oppose a project that the State or the world supports, or the reverse.
notes.tip: Every conflict answer needs both sides. An answer that describes only the damage is not about conflict, so always give the economic case and the environmental case.

notes.h: Who is involved
notes.b: Each conflict has several groups, called stakeholders (people or bodies affected by a decision), and they rarely agree. Knowing who they are lets you explain who wants what.
points: Developers and companies want to build or extract, and government and State agencies decide, regulate or sometimes carry out the project themselves.
Local communities are often divided among themselves, because some residents gain jobs or income while others lose quiet, safety or their way of life.
Environmental groups, farmers and fishermen, tourists, the EU and the courts are also involved. Farmers and fishermen depend on the land or sea, and the EU and the courts set and enforce the rules.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for a conflict between people, so name the groups on each side and what each wants.

notes.h: How conflicts are resolved
notes.b: Conflicts are settled through legal and planning systems, through payment, or through a deal that gives each side part of what it wants.
points: Planning permission (official approval to build) is needed for most developments, and decisions can be appealed to An Coimisiún Pleanála (formerly An Bord Pleanála), the national planning appeals body.
An environmental impact assessment (a study of a project's likely effects on the environment) is carried out before approval, and court cases follow where decisions are challenged.
EU law, such as the Habitats and Birds Directives, protects habitats and species, so a member state must protect them even when it would prefer to develop.
Compensation can be paid, such as payments to turf cutters or to fishermen who give up fishing, to make a restriction acceptable to those who lose by it.
Compromise includes route changes, limits on activity, conditions attached to permission and sustainable management (using a resource so that it lasts).

notes.h: Corrib gas: the economic case
notes.b: The Corrib gas project is a national example of a conflict. Gas from a field under the sea promised energy and money, but bringing it ashore caused a long local dispute.
points: The Corrib gas field lies about 80 km off north-west Co. Mayo and was discovered in 1996.
Gas first flowed in December 2015 and, so that it could be used, was processed at the Bellanaboy terminal (the onshore plant that treats the gas); for a time it supplied over half of Ireland's gas.
Economic arguments were energy security (less reliance on imported gas), a domestic gas supply, revenue for the State and the companies, and construction jobs.
notes.tip: Use the Corrib facts about the field only to set up the conflict, then spend your answer on the two sides, the groups involved and the outcome.

notes.h: Corrib gas: local and environmental objections
notes.b: Opposition came from how and where the gas would be brought ashore, not from the field itself.
points: The original plan piped high-pressure, unprocessed gas onshore near homes at Rossport, creating a safety risk for residents because raw gas at high pressure is dangerous close to houses.
The Shell to Sea campaign, from 2005, argued that the gas should be processed at sea rather than onshore, which would keep the hazardous raw gas away from people.
Sruwaddacon Bay, a protected estuary (a Special Area of Conservation, a site protected under EU law for its habitats), lay on the route of the pipeline.

notes.h: Corrib gas: protests, changes and outcome
notes.b: The dispute escalated into jailings and years of protest before the project was altered and completed.
points: The Rossport Five were jailed in June 2005 for refusing to obey a court order not to obstruct pipeline work; they were released after 94 days.
Protests were policed heavily for years, and the dispute divided the local community, because some residents backed the project and others opposed it.
The onshore route was changed to keep the pipeline further from houses, and a tunnel was bored under Sruwaddacon Bay to carry it, so the protected estuary was not dug up.
Shell sold its share in the project in 2018.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: fishing communities and EU quotas
notes.b: Fish in Irish waters are a shared resource. Fishing communities want a bigger catch, while conservation rules limit how much can be taken.
points: Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port, so it matters most for jobs; the six State Fishery Harbour Centres are Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel, Dunmore East and Howth. Coastal jobs depend on these harbours.
Under the Common Fisheries Policy (1983), total allowable catches (the maximum amount of each species that may be caught) are set by the EU and divided into national quotas.
Irish fishermen have long argued that Ireland's share of the catch in its own rich waters is too small, and much of that catch is taken by other EU fleets.
Ireland's exclusive economic zone (the sea area where the State has the rights to the resources) extends 200 nautical miles from the coast.
notes.tip: Keep to the conflict between fishing jobs and conservation limits. Quotas are the point of contention here, so show who wants more fish and who wants fewer taken.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: Brexit and decommissioning
notes.b: Political change after Brexit (the UK leaving the EU) shrank what Irish boats could catch, which hurt fishing incomes.
points: The EU-UK Brexit trade agreement (December 2020) reduced Irish quotas, so Irish boats were allowed to catch less.
A scheme paid vessel owners to decommission (scrap) their boats, which cut the size of the fleet to match the smaller quota.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: the wild salmon drift-net ban
notes.b: When wild salmon numbers collapsed, the State banned a fishing method, which set commercial fishermen against anglers and conservationists.
points: Ireland banned drift-net fishing (fishing with nets left floating in the open sea) for wild salmon at sea from 2007, because wild salmon returning to Irish rivers had fallen sharply.
Commercial salmon fishermen received compensation, so that they were not left without income, for losing their livelihood.
Anglers (people who fish with rods) and conservation groups supported the ban, because wild salmon sustain angling tourism.
notes.tip: This example is a conflict between commercial fishermen on one side and conservation and angling tourism on the other, so name both.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: mackerel dispute and fish farming
notes.b: Fish stocks cross borders and farms share water with wild fish, so conflicts reach beyond Ireland and affect the sea and the bays.
points: From 2010 Iceland and the Faroe Islands set large mackerel quotas as mackerel moved north-west into their waters, taking a bigger share of a stock Irish boats also fish.

The EU, with strong support from Irish fishermen, protested; in 2013 it imposed trade measures on the Faroe Islands over its herring catches, banning imports of Faroese herring and mackerel; the dispute eased in 2014.
Salmon farms in western bays are blamed by anglers for harming wild salmon and sea trout, because sea lice (parasites that attach to fish) from the farms spread to wild fish.

notes.h: Mullaghmore, the Burren: the proposed visitor centre
notes.b: Mullaghmore is a main national case of tourism against a fragile landscape. A visitor centre was meant to help tourism but was planned in a place valued for being unspoilt.
points: The Burren, Co. Clare, has Carboniferous limestone pavement (a bare, flat surface of limestone), with rare Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants growing side by side, such as spring gentian and mountain avens.
Mullaghmore is a hill of folded, terraced limestone; the Burren National Park protects the area near it.

In the early 1990s the Office of Public Works (OPW, the State body that manages heritage sites and public buildings) began building an interpretative centre (a visitor centre with displays) and car park near Mullaghmore.
notes.tip: The Burren is a protected landscape, not a quarrying area, and Mullaghmore is in Co. Clare. Do not invent a final location for the visitor centre.

notes.h: Mullaghmore: the two sides
notes.b: The two sides disagreed on whether a visitor centre at Mullaghmore would help or harm the Burren, because one side focused on jobs and income and the other on the fragile landscape.
points: Supporters wanted tourism jobs and visitor spending in a poor rural area, and better visitor management, which means directing visitors to one place instead of leaving them to wander.
The Burren Action Group argued that traffic, sewage and visitor pressure would damage a fragile, unspoilt landscape, and that any centre should be in nearby villages.

notes.h: Mullaghmore: legal challenge and outcome
notes.b: The case was settled in the courts and the planning system, so it shows how legal challenge can stop a State project.
points: In 1993 the Supreme Court (Ireland's highest court) ruled that the State had to obtain planning permission like any other developer, so the State was not exempt from the planning rules, and work stopped.
In 2000 An Bord Pleanála refused permission, and the partly built site was cleared and restored.

notes.h: Skellig Michael: heritage and its setting
notes.b: Skellig Michael is a remote island of great heritage and wildlife value, which is why increased tourism there is a problem.
points: Skellig Michael, about 12 km off the Iveragh Peninsula, Co. Kerry, has an early Christian monastery of stone beehive huts on a steep rocky island.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place recognised by the United Nations as being of outstanding value to humanity) since 1996 and is managed by the OPW.
Seabirds, including puffins, Manx shearwaters and storm petrels, breed on the island; Little Skellig holds one of the world's largest gannet colonies.
notes.tip: Skellig Michael is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Little Skellig cannot be landed on, and the only visitor figure to give is about 180 a day.

notes.h: Skellig Michael: tourism pressures and management
notes.b: Film fame brought more demand for visits than a fragile island can easily take, so access is controlled.
points: Filming for the Star Wars films (from 2014) greatly increased demand for visits.
Boat operators and local businesses want more access, because visitors bring them income; conservationists object to the filming and to rising visitor numbers.
Access is only by licensed boats in summer, with visitor numbers capped at about 180 a day; landings depend on the weather.
Steep steps and the weather make landing a safety issue, which is why landings are limited.

notes.h: Hill of Tara: heritage
notes.b: The Hill of Tara is a heritage site of national importance, and the land around it is rich in archaeology. This is the heritage side of the conflict over the M3 motorway.
points: The Hill of Tara, Co. Meath, is an ancient ceremonial site and the traditional seat of the High Kings of Ireland.

The Tara-Skryne valley around the hill is an archaeological landscape (an area where the sites and the land together tell the story of the past); excavation along the planned road route found dozens of sites.

notes.h: M3 motorway: the economic case
notes.b: The road was meant to solve a transport problem for fast-growing towns, and the best route crossed an important archaeological area.
points: The M3 runs from Clonee to north of Kells, relieving congestion on the N3 for the fast-growing commuter towns of Meath (towns whose residents travel to work elsewhere), such as Navan and Kells.
It cuts journey times to Dublin, so commuters save time, which helps regional access and commuters.
The route passes through the Tara-Skryne valley, about 2 km from the Hill of Tara.

notes.h: M3 and the Hill of Tara: objections and outcome
notes.b: Opponents said the road would destroy archaeology. The road was built, but only after a major find was recorded.
points: Campaign groups, archaeologists and protesters camped on the route argued that the road would destroy an archaeological landscape.
In 2007 a large prehistoric ceremonial enclosure was found at Lismullin and declared a national monument; it was excavated and recorded, and then the road was built over it.
The M3 opened in 2010, so the road was completed despite the protests.
notes.tip: The Lismullin site was excavated and recorded and the road built over it. Do not say it was preserved in place or that the route was changed.

notes.h: Turf cutting on protected raised bogs: the conflict
notes.b: Turf (dried peat cut from bogs) is a traditional fuel, but the bogs it comes from are rare habitats protected by EU law.
points: Turf cutting gives rural families a traditional right and a cheap source of fuel.
Raised bogs are rare in Europe and store large amounts of carbon; Ireland holds a large share of the EU's remaining active raised bog (bog that is still growing).
The EU Habitats Directive (1992) required Ireland to designate raised bogs as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs), sites protected for their habitats.

notes.h: Turf cutting on protected raised bogs: ban, compensation and protest
notes.b: The ban took away a traditional way of life, so the State offered compensation. Even so, some people protested.
points: After a ten-year derogation (a temporary exemption from the rules) ended, turf cutting was banned on 53 raised-bog SACs from 2011.
Compensation: about €1,500 a year for 15 years per turf cutter, or relocation to a bog that is not protected.
The Turf Cutters and Contractors Association organised protests, because the ban ended a traditional right, and some cutting continued on some bogs.

notes.h: Wind farms: renewables against local interests
notes.b: Wind power helps with climate targets, but turbines are built in places where people live and wildlife lives, so wind farms cause conflict at local and national level.
points: Economic and renewable case: renewable energy targets, income for landowners and community funds. The Climate Action Plan aims for 80% renewable electricity by 2030.
Local objections: visual impact, noise, shadow flicker (the flickering shadow cast by rotating blades), falling property values, effects on birds, and peat stability.
Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway: a peat slide of about 450,000 m³ on 16 October 2003, during wind-farm construction, killed fish in the Owendalulleegh River.
In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland €5 million plus €15,000 a day because no proper environmental impact assessment (a study of effects before approval) had been carried out.
Offshore wind: the Climate Action Plan sets at least 5 GW (gigawatts, a measure of generating capacity) of offshore wind, which can conflict with fishing grounds and seascapes.
notes.tip: Derrybrien is in Co. Galway, not Co. Clare. Do not use invented wind-farm sites in an answer.

notes.h: Dairy expansion, water and climate
notes.b: Ending milk quotas let farmers produce more milk. The economic gain came with costs for rivers and for the climate.
points: Milk quotas (EU limits on how much milk each farmer could produce) were abolished on 1 April 2015, and the dairy herd grew strongly afterwards.
Economic case: farm incomes and food exports, because more milk means more to sell.
Environmental case: nitrates (chemicals from fertiliser and slurry) reaching water damage water quality; agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions.

EPA (the Environmental Protection Agency, 2016-2021): only about half of Irish rivers, lakes and estuaries were in good or high ecological status (a measure of water health), with agriculture the main pressure.
Sectoral ceilings (limits on emissions set for each sector of the economy, 2022) require agriculture to cut emissions by 25% by 2030.

notes.h: Data centres and electricity
notes.b: Data centres (buildings full of computers that store and process online data) bring investment, but they use so much electricity that they conflict with climate goals.
points: Economic case: investment, multinational jobs and Ireland's technology economy, because the centres bring in big companies.
Data centres used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO, the Central Statistics Office), and most are in the Dublin region.
Environmental and grid case: huge electricity demand strains the grid (the national network that carries electricity) and works against climate targets.
In 2022 EirGrid (the operator of the electricity grid) said it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin area until about 2028, because the grid could not supply them.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: economic drivers
notes.b: The Amazon is the main global example. Brazil's economic activities clear the forest for farming, timber, mining, roads and power.
points: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, with about 60% of it in Brazil.
Cattle ranching is the main driver of clearing, and most cleared land becomes pasture; soya farming spreads in the south.
Logging removes timber from the forest, so the trees are cut for sale, for example.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway, begun in 1970, opened the forest to settlers; clearings along the roads form a fishbone pattern (a central road with side tracks branching off), as in Rondônia.
Carajás, Pará, has the world's largest iron-ore mine, run by Vale.
The Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River, completed in 2019, was opposed by indigenous groups including the Kayapó.
notes.tip: Keep the Amazon as a conflict of interests: pair each economic driver with the environmental interest it threatens.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: environmental and global interests
notes.b: The forest matters to people far from Brazil, so protecting it is a global interest as well as a Brazilian one.
points: The forest holds biodiversity (a huge variety of species), stores large amounts of carbon, recycles rainfall and is home to indigenous peoples.
Global interest: clearing the forest releases carbon that adds to climate change, while Brazil's development needs drive clearing.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: deforestation trend
notes.b: Satellite figures show how clearing fell when protection was strong and rose when it weakened. These are rounded figures for the Brazilian Amazon only.
points: Satellite monitoring by PRODES (Brazil's official programme for measuring deforestation): about 27,800 km² of the Brazilian Amazon was cleared in 2004.
Clearing was cut by over 80%, to about 4,600 km², by 2012, showing that protection can work.
Clearing rose again to about 13,000 km² in 2021, so the gains were not permanent.
notes.tip: Keep the years exactly as given and give no later yearly figure.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: protection measures and policy swings
notes.b: Brazil and other countries have tried several ways to slow clearing, but results have depended on which government is in power.
points: Brazil's Forest Code, a law to protect the forest, requires landowners in the Amazon to keep 80% of their land as forest, though this is often not enforced.
The soy moratorium (an agreed pause) of 2006: major traders agreed not to buy soya from newly cleared Amazon land.
The Amazon Fund of 2008: donors, mainly Norway and also Germany, pay for reduced deforestation.
Deforestation rose under President Bolsonaro (2019-2022) and fell under President Lula (2003-2010, and again from 2023), showing that government policy matters.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: people in conflict
notes.b: The Amazon conflict was also a conflict between people, sometimes with deadly results.
points: Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper (a worker who collects rubber from trees without felling them) and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988.
His murder shows that the conflict over clearing was one between people, not only between economic and environmental interests.
notes.tip: Chico Mendes was murdered in 1988; the Rio Earth Summit was 1992. Do not merge them. Ordinary Level questions ask for a conflict between people, so this case suits them.

notes.h: Lignite mining in Germany: the Hambach Forest
notes.b: Germany is a European example of a global conflict: mining a fuel that heats the climate against protecting a forest and villages.
points: RWE's Hambach open-cast lignite mine (a surface mine for lignite, a soft brown coal) in North Rhine-Westphalia expands into the ancient Hambach Forest.
Economic side: the mine supplies power and jobs in the Rhineland. Environmental side: the forest, the villages and the carbon released by burning lignite.
Protesters occupied tree houses in the forest for years, to stop the trees being felled; in October 2018 a German court halted the clearing.
The remaining forest was later spared under the coal phase-out (the planned ending of coal use).
notes.tip: Lützerath and Hambach are in Germany's Rhineland lignite area, not the Black Triangle, which is a different example.

notes.h: Lignite mining in Germany: Lützerath and the coal phase-out
notes.b: Even after the Hambach ruling, mining continued elsewhere, until national law set an end date for coal.
points: The village of Lützerath was cleared of protesters in January 2023 to extend the Garzweiler lignite mine.
Germany's 2020 law ends coal-fired power by 2038 at the latest, so the mines have a fixed end date.

notes.h: Three Gorges Dam, China: benefits
notes.b: The Three Gorges Dam is a huge project that shows the economic case for damming a river.
points: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River is the world's largest power station by installed capacity (the most electricity it can generate).
It provides clean electricity, flood control downstream and improved navigation (easier passage for ships).
The dam was completed in 2006 and became fully operational in 2012.

notes.h: Three Gorges Dam, China: costs
notes.b: The same dam brought heavy costs for people, heritage and the river itself.
points: Over one million people were relocated, because the reservoir flooded their homes.
Farmland, towns and archaeological sites were flooded by the reservoir (the lake formed behind the dam).
The dam traps sediment that would otherwise reach the river downstream, and the ecology of the river has changed.

notes.h: Global versus local interests in climate policy
notes.b: The conflict between economy and environment also shows up between countries, in the argument over who should cut emissions.
points: Developing countries argue for their right to develop with cheap energy, while the global need is to cut emissions.
Fossil-fuel exporting countries protect their revenue from coal, oil and gas, which they would lose if the world used less of them.
Belém, Pará, hosted the COP30 climate conference in November 2025.

notes.h: Map-based question: locating a development
notes.b: On an Ordnance Survey map question you are asked to show how conflict could arise from where a development is placed. Work through the same steps each time.
points: Identify the development and the features of the site it needs, such as a wind farm on high ground with open views, or a quarry close to a village.
Read the map for relevant features, because they show who would be affected: contour lines for height, settlements, roads for access, rivers, and protected areas.
Identify the groups for and against: developers and landowners usually support a site, while residents, environmental groups and tourism businesses may object.
Conflict arises when a site serves one group's interests while threatening another group's interests; give the reasons for each side.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to locate a wind farm or similar development on an Ordnance Survey map and explain how conflict may arise, at Ordinary and Higher Level. Name the groups for and against and their reasons.

keyTerms.definition: A person or group with an interest in a development, such as a company, a community, a government agency or an environmental group.
A site protected under EU law for its habitats or species, such as the raised bogs and estuaries designated in Ireland.
A bog that rises above the surrounding land and stores large amounts of carbon, and is rare in Europe.
An exemption from a law for a set period, such as the ten-year period that allowed turf cutting on protected raised bogs.
A net left hanging in the water to catch fish, banned in Ireland for wild salmon at sea from 2007.
A soft brown coal, mined in open-cast pits in Germany's Rhineland and burned to generate electricity.
Parasites from salmon farms that are blamed by anglers for harming wild salmon and sea trout.
A visitor building that explains a site's natural or historic features, such as the one planned near Mullaghmore.

questions.prompt: Discuss how conflict may develop between economic interests and environmental interests, with reference to two examples that you have studied.
questions.model: Corrib gas, Co. Mayo: the economic case was a domestic gas supply from the field about 80 km off north-west Co. Mayo, which for a time supplied over half of Ireland's gas, with revenue and construction jobs. The local and environmental case objected to piping high-pressure, unprocessed gas onshore near homes at Rossport, and to the risk to Sruwaddacon Bay, a protected estuary. The Shell to Sea campaign from 2005 argued the gas should be processed at sea. The Rossport Five were jailed in June 2005 for defying a court order and were released after 94 days, and protests were heavily policed for years, dividing the community. The onshore route was changed and a tunnel was bored under Sruwaddacon Bay; gas first flowed in December 2015, and Shell sold its share in 2018. Irish fish stocks: fishing communities at ports such as Killybegs depend on quotas set under the Common Fisheries Policy, and Irish fishermen argue Ireland's share of its own rich waters is too small. Brexit reduced Irish quotas and led to vessel decommissioning. Conservation measures, such as the 2007 ban on wild salmon drift-netting, cost commercial fishermen compensation, while anglers and conservationists supported it. The mackerel and herring disputes with Iceland and the Faroe Islands led to EU trade measures against the Faroes in 2013, and sea lice from salmon farms harm wild salmon and sea trout.

questions.prompt: Examine one global example of conflict between economic development and environmental interests.
questions.model: The Amazon rainforest, Brazil. Economic drivers include cattle ranching, which is the main cause of clearing, soya farming in the south, logging, the Carajás iron-ore mine run by Vale, the Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River completed in 2019, and the Trans-Amazonian Highway begun in 1970, which opened the forest to settlers and created the fishbone pattern of clearings seen in Rondônia. Environmental interests include biodiversity, the carbon the forest stores, rainfall recycling and the land of indigenous peoples such as the Kayapó, who opposed Belo Monte. Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon, measured by PRODES, was about 27,800 km² in 2004, was cut by over 80% to about 4,600 km² by 2012, and rose again to about 13,000 km² in 2021. Protection measures include Brazil's Forest Code requiring 80% forest on Amazon landholdings, though often not enforced, the soy moratorium of 2006, the Amazon Fund of 2008 paid for mainly by Norway and also Germany, and indigenous reserves. Policy has swung with the government: clearing rose under President Bolsonaro (2019–2022) and fell under President Lula. Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988, showing how the conflict was fought between people.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one example of how the development of economic activities has resulted in conflict between people. (ii) Describe and explain this conflict.
questions.model: Mullaghmore, the Burren, Co. Clare: the Office of Public Works began building an interpretative centre and car park near Mullaghmore in the early 1990s. Supporters argued that tourism would bring jobs and spending to a poor rural area and allow better visitor management. The Burren Action Group argued that traffic, sewage and visitor pressure would damage the fragile limestone landscape with its rare Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants, and that any centre should be in nearby villages. The conflict between people became a legal one: in 1993 the Supreme Court ruled that the State needed planning permission like any other developer, and work stopped. In 2000 An Bord Pleanála refused permission, and the partly built site was cleared and restored.
